title: Quality management
overview: Quality management aims to deliver outputs fit for purpose and consistent with customer expectations. You must distinguish quality control, quality assurance and Total Quality Management and explain how benchmarking can identify performance gaps and support improvement.
syllabusPoints: Explain why quality matters and how customer expectations define appropriate quality.
Explain the purpose, process and limitations of benchmarking.

definitions.definition: Inspection/testing of output to identify defects, often after or at stages of production.
Systems and procedures designed to prevent defects by building quality into processes.
A whole-organisation culture of continuous quality improvement where everyone is responsible for quality.
Comparing performance/processes with a strong external or internal reference to identify improvement gaps.
Ongoing repeated efforts to improve process, quality, cost or customer value.

sections.title: Why quality matters
content: Consistent quality can reduce returns/rework, strengthen reputation, support repeat purchase and premium positioning, and reduce waste. But 'maximum specification' is not always optimal if customers will not pay for it; quality is about meeting target expectations reliably.

sections.title: Quality control
content: Inspection detects defects before they reach customers and provides measurable standards. It can be expensive and often finds errors after resources have already been wasted; responsibility may become concentrated in inspectors rather than the workforce.

sections.title: Quality assurance
content: Standards, procedures, training and process checks aim to prevent errors at source. It can improve consistency and reduce rework but requires design, documentation, staff commitment and supplier consistency.

sections.title: Total Quality Management
content: TQM makes quality everyone's responsibility and emphasises customer focus, prevention and continuous improvement. Potential gains include lower defect cost and stronger culture; barriers include training/time cost, employee resistance and difficulty maintaining commitment.

sections.title: Benchmarking process
content: Identify what to improve, select a comparator/best practice, measure gaps, understand the reasons, adapt practices, implement and review. It can provide external targets but data may be unavailable and blindly copying another firm can fail because objectives/resources differ.

sections.title: Quality and finance/strategy
content: Quality investment can raise short-run costs but reduce warranty, scrap and complaint costs and improve demand/reputation. The judgement depends on defect cost, customer expectations, competitive position and required investment.

analysisChains.title: Total Quality Management
steps: Every employee takes responsibility for quality
Waste, rework and complaints may fall
Reputation and repeat purchasing may improve
analysisChains.evaluation: TQM needs long-term cultural commitment; training costs and employee resistance can outweigh gains if implementation is superficial.

examTips: Quality control = detection; quality assurance = prevention/process design.
TQM answers should include everyone + customer focus + continuous improvement.
Link quality to revenue/reputation AND cost/rework effects.
commonMistakes: Treating benchmarking as copying without adaptation.
